01-what-inference-engineering-is-m1: Three layers of an inference request: the agent loop, retry policy, and prompt assembly in the harness feed a provider gateway, queue, and serving engine, which repeatedly reads fixed model weights and streams tokens back.
01-what-inference-engineering-is-m2: The nine-stage request path runs from JSON serialization and network setup through admission, routing, queueing, prefill, serial decode, streaming, and final billing. Rejected requests stop at admission before reaching a GPU.
02-the-shape-of-a-token-m1: Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel, but decode is serial: step one emits token one, each later step reads the model again, and the process advances one token at a time until the stop token.
02-the-shape-of-a-token-m2: With time to first token fixed at 0.4 seconds, end-to-end latency rises linearly with output length. At 500 tokens it is 25.4 seconds at 50 milliseconds per token, 12.9 seconds at 25 milliseconds, and 5.4 seconds at 10 milliseconds.
03-the-arithmetic-of-waiting-m1: The H100 BF16 roofline rises with arithmetic intensity from zero to about 989 trillion operations per second at 295 operations per byte, then stays flat because compute capacity, rather than memory bandwidth, becomes the limit.
04-the-memory-that-is-not-the-model-m1: KV-cache memory grows linearly with context length. From 8,000 to 128,000 tokens, a Llama 3.1 8B session grows from 1 to 16 GiB, while a Llama 3.1 70B session grows from 2.5 to 40 GiB.
05-batches-the-engines-trick-m1: A continuous-batching scheduler repeatedly forms an iteration, runs one token step for every active request, retires requests that emitted an end marker, frees their KV blocks, and immediately admits waiting requests into the open slots.
05-batches-the-engines-trick-m2: As offered load rises, raw throughput climbs and plateaus near 44 requests per second. Goodput, which counts only requests meeting latency bounds, peaks near 29 and then falls to 6 as overload makes more completions too late.
06-paging-the-brain-m1: Two requests map logical prompt blocks into noncontiguous GPU-memory slots. Their identical two-block system prompt shares slots 17 and 42, while their different user turns occupy separate slots 9 and 61.
07-prefill-decode-great-divorce-m1: Without chunking, a long prefill creates one 420-millisecond token-time spike in an otherwise 15-millisecond decode stream. Splitting prefill into 2,048-token chunks spreads the work into several roughly 21-to-23-millisecond iterations.
07-prefill-decode-great-divorce-m2: A client sends its prompt to a compute-bound prefill pool sized for time-to-first-token goals. The resulting KV state moves to a bandwidth-bound decode pool sized for per-token goals, while a DRAM or SSD tier can retain reusable KV state.
08-guessing-at-the-speed-of-light-m1: Speculative decoding loops through a cheap drafter proposing several tokens, one target-model pass verifying them together, and a left-to-right rejection sampler. Accepted guesses advance; the first disagreement is resampled and discards every later guess.
08-guessing-at-the-speed-of-light-m2: For four drafted tokens, expected progress per target-model verification rises nonlinearly with acceptance: from 1.25 tokens at a 0.2 acceptance rate to 2.31 at 0.6 and 4.10 at 0.9.
09-smaller-numbers-faster-engines-m1: BF16 KV cache starts cheaper than FP8 because FP8 has conversion overhead, but BF16 cost rises faster as cached context grows. The lines cross near 7,000 cached tokens, after which FP8 is cheaper per decoded token.
09-smaller-numbers-faster-engines-m2: A model-variant decision tree first asks whether precision is labeled, then routes by task. Quantized variants suit short, high-volume classification; math and code stay at FP8 or better; long histories favor KV quantization, followed by pinned versions and recurring evaluation.
10-one-model-many-chips-m1: Incoming requests split across two data-parallel replicas. Inside each replica, work crosses two pipeline stages made of two-chip tensor-parallel groups, with an expert-parallel strip handling routed mixture-of-experts work in the second stage.
11-long-context-is-a-memory-product-m1: Gemini 3.1 Pro input cost rises at two dollars per million tokens through 199,000 tokens, reaching about 40 cents, then jumps at the 200,000-token pricing boundary to about 80 cents and continues at four dollars per million, reaching two dollars at 500,000 tokens.
11-long-context-is-a-memory-product-m2: Measured recall of injected facts falls as more of a 190,000-token context is compacted: 73 percent with no compaction, 40 percent when half is compacted, and 7 percent when 98 percent is compacted.
11-long-context-is-a-memory-product-m3: A context-budget decision tree asks whether many turns remain. If not, trim or end using retrieval and checkpoints; if yes, compact at a turn boundary, copy critical constraints and identifiers verbatim, pay one full re-prefill, and verify the summary with a canary task.
12-the-streaming-contract-m1: Four provider stream grammars—OpenAI Chat chunks, OpenAI Responses events, Anthropic block events, and Gemini response chunks—converge on one normalizer that emits text deltas, tool-call deltas, usage, and stop-reason events.
12-the-streaming-contract-m2: With a 0.4-second first-token time, streaming keeps the wait for something readable flat at 0.4 seconds regardless of output length. Without streaming, perceived wait grows to 5.4 seconds for a 200-token reply.
13-structured-output-is-not-a-prompt-tri: The constrained-sampling pipeline applies history penalties to model logits, masks grammar-illegal tokens, adjusts temperature, truncates to allowed top candidates, samples one token, advances the grammar state, and repeats for the next model step.
14-the-cache-that-pays-your-bill-m1: Across a 25-turn agent loop, no caching has the highest and steadily rising input cost. Prefix-only caching lowers the parallel middle line, while incremental caching drops after its first write and remains nearly flat, ending around 4,450 base-input units per turn.
14-the-cache-that-pays-your-bill-m2: Cache invalidation follows byte position: editing a tool definition invalidates tools, system prompt, and messages; editing the system prompt invalidates it and all messages; editing an early message invalidates later messages; appending a message preserves the existing prefix.
15-rate-limits-are-physics-m1: A retry decision tree reads both status and error type. Billing or quota failures stop immediately; rate limits honor Retry-After or use jitter; overloads, timeouts, and server errors use jitter; every path stops when the attempt or time budget is spent and then sheds or reroutes load.
15-rate-limits-are-physics-m2: Queue residence time accelerates as quota utilization approaches saturation: about 1.4 service-times at 30 percent, 2 at 50 percent, 5 at 80 percent, 10 at 90 percent, and 20 at 95 percent utilization.
16-routing-fallbacks-money-meter-m1: A circuit breaker cycles through closed, open, and half-open. Failure thresholds open it and block wire calls; a cooldown permits limited probes; a successful probe closes it, while a failed probe reopens it.
16-routing-fallbacks-money-meter-m2: For a 10,000-request nightly fanout, cost falls as prefix-cache hits rise. Interactive cost drops from 120 dollars at zero hits to 79.50 dollars at full hits; batch cost drops from 60 dollars to 39.75 dollars and stays cheaper throughout.
17-cache-aware-harness-design-m1: Without compaction, cumulative input cost rises 15,000 token-equivalents per turn to 150,000 after ten turns. Compacting a 150,000-token context to 30,000 starts with a 30,000-token rewrite but rises only 3,000 per turn, breaking even during the third turn.
17-cache-aware-harness-design-m2: A compaction-timing decision tree compacts before a long idle gap while the cache is warm, otherwise keeps the transcript append-only until the context window approaches. After a cold resume it replays bytes verbatim and avoids paying to summarize expired history.
17-cache-aware-harness-design-m3: A session cache state machine loops while warm, becomes evicted after its time-to-live expires, and returns through a full-price cold rebuild. Forks can reuse a shared prefix cheaply, while template changes trigger a herd event that makes every session cold together.
17-cache-aware-harness-design-m4: A parent session keeps its cached head while spawning children. The first child pays to write its own head, later siblings can read the shared preamble cheaply, byte-identical forks inherit the parent prefix, and divergence from the first byte loses all inheritance.
18-your-own-engine-room-m1: The assembled tinyengine path runs from agent loop through a five-layer prompt assembler, quota-aware scheduler, router, and hosted or local endpoints; normalized stream events feed a cache-cost ledger and session store, while latency traces and lifecycle prices feed the next turn.
appendix-d-tinyengine-companion-m1: The companion wiring sends the agent loop through SessionStore, RateScheduler, and Router to either hosted or local endpoints. StreamNormalizer unifies both outputs, the tracer records timing, CacheLedger prices usage and expiry, and the ledger feeds session state.
